literal: Ju pointed at Xiuyi and said: "This one seated above—he violates the Son of Heaven's clear edict; whoever has more goods gets office. Daylight robbery in the capital— is this not a great thief?"
idiomatic: Ju pointed at Xiuyi and said, "The man seated there violates the Son of Heaven's clear edict—whoever brings more goods gets office. Robbery in broad daylight at the capital—is that not the greatest thief of all?"

literal: Xiuyi turned pale.
idiomatic: Xiuyi turned pale.

literal: Ju went out cursing; later he wished to intercept the imperial carriage to argue Xiuyi's crimes, but Left Vice Director Xiao Baoyin persuaded him and he stopped.
idiomatic: Ju stormed out still cursing; later he meant to waylay the imperial carriage to denounce Xiuyi's crimes, but Left Vice Director Xiao Baoyin talked him out of it.

literal: When the two Qins rebelled, Xiuyi was provisionally made Right Vice Director of the Masters of Writing, Western Route Commissioner, and acting Governor of Qin Province, commanding all armies.
idiomatic: When the two Qin provinces rebelled, Xiuyi was made acting Right Vice Director of the Masters of Writing, Western Route Commissioner, and acting Governor of Qin, with command over all forces.

literal: Xiuyi by nature loved wine; each bout of drinking lasted many days, and he then met wind illness—his spirit dim and lost—so that though he reached Chang'an he ultimately brought no benefit of disposition.
idiomatic: Xiuyi loved wine; each bout lasted days on end until wind illness struck and his mind grew clouded, so that though he reached Chang'an he could offer no effective command.

literal: Yuan Zhi was defeated and perished; the rebels advanced east to Heishui; they again sent Xiao Baoyin to campaign, with Xiuyi as Governor of Yong Province.
idiomatic: When Yuan Zhi was defeated and killed the rebels advanced east to Heishui; Xiao Baoyin was again sent against them, with Xiuyi as Governor of Yong.

literal: He died in the province; posthumously made Minister of Works; his posthumous title was Wen.
idiomatic: He died in office and was posthumously made Minister of Works with the posthumous title Wen.

literal: His son Jun held the office of Attendant of the Yellow Gate in charge of matters.
idiomatic: His son Jun served as Attendant of the Yellow Gate in charge of matters.

literal: Later he entered Western Wei, was enfeoffed Prince of Anchang, and held the rank of Defender-in-Chief with the same ceremony as the Three Dukes.
idiomatic: Later he entered Western Wei, was enfeoffed Prince of Anchang, and held Defender-in-Chief with Three-Duke ceremony.

literal: At his death he was posthumously made Minister of Works; his posthumous title was Ping.
idiomatic: At his death he was posthumously made Minister of Works with the posthumous title Ping.

literal: His son Ze, courtesy name Xiaogui, inherited the title and held the office of Governor of Yi Province.
idiomatic: His son Ze, courtesy name Xiaogui, inherited the title and served as Governor of Yi Province.

literal: Serving Zhou he was Junior Director of the Mausoleum and Commander-in-Chief of Jiangling.
idiomatic: Under Zhou he was Junior Director of the Mausoleum and Commander-in-Chief of Jiangling.

literal: Soon afterward Yuwen Huaji established the Prince of Qin Hao as emperor and led troops to Pengcheng; wherever he passed the land trembled.
idiomatic: Soon afterward Yuwen Huaji set up Prince Hao of Qin as emperor and marched to Pengcheng; the land shook wherever his army passed.

literal: Wendu persuaded Tong to send envoys to Li Mi.
idiomatic: Wendu persuaded Yang Tong to send envoys to Li Mi.

literal: Mi then requested surrender and was thereupon granted office and rank; Tong treated his envoys with great courtesy.
idiomatic: Li Mi then offered to submit and was granted office and rank; Tong treated his envoys with great honor.

literal: Wang Shichong was displeased; Wendu knew it and secretly formed a plan to kill Shichong.
idiomatic: Wang Shichong was displeased; Wendu knew it and secretly plotted to kill him.

literal: Tong made Wendu oversee the Censorate; Shichong firmly opposed it and stopped it.
idiomatic: Tong wished to put Wendu in charge of the Censorate, but Shichong firmly blocked it.

literal: Lu Chu urged Wendu to kill him; Wendu then entered the hall bearing a memorial.
idiomatic: Lu Chu urged Wendu to kill Shichong; Wendu then entered the hall with a memorial.

literal: Someone informed Shichong; Shichong galloped back to Jiahe Fortress.
idiomatic: Someone informed Shichong; he galloped back to Jiahe Fortress.

literal: At night trouble arose; he attacked through the East Sun Gate and entered, bowing below the Ziwei Observatory, saying: "I beg to behead Wendu and return the blame to the Minister of Justice."
idiomatic: That night rebellion broke out; he forced the East Sun Gate and entered, bowing below the Ziwei Observatory: "I beg leave to behead Wendu and lay the blame on the Minister of Justice."

literal: Tong, seeing the troops' strength, sent the general he had appointed, Huang Taoshu, to seize Wendu and bring him out.
idiomatic: Seeing the troops' strength, Tong sent his appointed general Huang Taoshu to seize Wendu and hand him over.

literal: Wendu turned and said to Tong: "Your servant dies this morning; Your Majesty will follow this evening."
idiomatic: Wendu turned to Tong and said, "I die this morning; Your Majesty will follow this evening."

literal: Tong wept as he sent him forth; those at his side were all silent in grief.
idiomatic: Tong wept as he sent him out; none beside him could speak for grief.

literal: When they reached Xingjiao Gate, Shichong ordered his attendants to hack him to pieces at random; his sons were all killed as well.
idiomatic: At Xingjiao Gate Shichong ordered his men to cut Wendu down; his sons were killed as well.

literal: Ze's younger brother Ju, courtesy name Xiaoju, in Western Wei inherited the grandfather's title as Duke of Shiping County and was appointed Governor of Nanfeng.
idiomatic: Ze's younger brother Ju, courtesy name Xiaoju, in Western Wei inherited their grandfather's title as Duke of Shiping and was appointed Governor of Nanfeng.

literal: Seeing the Yuan clan about to fall, he secretly told his brothers: "The heart of the Yuwen clan is plain to every passerby."
idiomatic: Seeing the Yuan house about to fall, he secretly told his brothers, "The Yuwen clan's intent is plain to every passerby."

literal: "When the house topples and you do not support it—of what use are the sons of the clan!"
idiomatic: "When the house topples and you will not prop it up—what use are the sons of the clan!"

literal: His elder brother Ze restrained him, and he stopped.
idiomatic: His elder brother Ze restrained him, and he desisted.

literal: Later Zhou Emperor Wen for his nephew the Duke of Jin, Hu, took Ju's younger sister as wife; their affection was very close.
idiomatic: Later Emperor Wen of Zhou took Ju's younger sister as wife for his nephew, the Duke of Jin, Hu; their bond was very close.

literal: When Hu was executed he was banished to Shu on account of it.
idiomatic: When Hu was executed Ju was banished to Shu on account of the connection.

literal: Later he was made Grand Master of the Ministry of Justice.
idiomatic: Later he was made Grand Master of the Ministry of Justice.

literal: Emperor Wen of Sui valued his family's standing and took his daughter as consort to the Prince of Fangling.
idiomatic: Emperor Wen of Sui valued his family's standing and married his daughter to the Prince of Fangling.

literal: When he became Chancellor he was made Junior Director of the Mausoleum, Pillar of State, and granted the title Duke of Xunyang Commandery.
idiomatic: When he became Chancellor he was made Junior Director of the Mausoleum and Pillar of State, and enfeoffed Duke of Xunyang.

literal: When the Prince of Fangling was established as Crown Prince, his daughter was made Crown Princess; the intimate courtesy grew thicker, and he was made Commander-in-Chief of Shou Province.
idiomatic: When the Prince of Fangling was made crown prince, Ju's daughter became crown princess; favor deepened and he was made Commander-in-Chief of Shou.

literal: At that time Chen generals Ren Mannu and others repeatedly raided north of the Yangtze; Xiaoju was again made overall commander on campaign, stationing troops on the river.
idiomatic: When Chen generals such as Ren Mannu repeatedly raided north of the Yangtze, Xiaoju was again made campaign commander-in-chief and stationed troops on the river.

literal: Later, because of age, he submitted a memorial begging to retire.
idiomatic: Later, owing to age, he memorialized to retire.

literal: He was made Governor of Jing Province.
idiomatic: He was made Governor of Jing Province.

literal: He died in office; his posthumous title was Jian.
idiomatic: He died in office with the posthumous title Jian.

literal: His son Wujie inherited.
idiomatic: His son Wujie inherited.

literal: Ju's next younger brother Ya, courtesy name Xiaofang, possessed civil and military ability.
idiomatic: Ju's next younger brother Ya, courtesy name Xiaofang, had both civil and military talent.

literal: In the Kaihuang era he successively served as General of the Left Guard, Governor of Ji and Qin Provinces, and was enfeoffed Duke of Shunyang Commandery.
idiomatic: Under Kaihuang he served as General of the Left Guard and Governor of Ji and Qin, and was enfeoffed Duke of Shunyang.

literal: Ya's younger brother Bao, courtesy name Xiaozheng, in youth had the measure of a grown man.
idiomatic: Ya's younger brother Bao, courtesy name Xiaozheng, even in youth had the stature of a man grown.

literal: At ten years he was orphaned and was cherished and raised by all his elder brothers.
idiomatic: Orphaned at ten, he was cherished and raised by all his elder brothers.

literal: He was good to all his elder brothers.
idiomatic: He treated all his elder brothers with devotion.

literal: When the elder brothers discussed separating households, Bao wept and remonstrated, but they did not follow.
idiomatic: When his brothers discussed dividing the household, Bao wept and remonstrated, but they would not listen.

literal: The family had long been wealthy with much gold and treasure; Bao accepted none of it and left empty-handed.
idiomatic: The family was long wealthy in gold and jewels; Bao took none of it and walked away with nothing.

literal: Serving Zhou he held the rank of Defender-in-Chief, Duke of Beiping County, and Governor of Zhao Province.
idiomatic: Under Zhou he was Defender-in-Chief, Duke of Beiping, and Governor of Zhao.

literal: Following Wei Xiaokuan in pacifying Yuchi Jiong, for merit he was made Pillar of State and advanced to Duke of Hejian Commandery.
idiomatic: Following Wei Xiaokuan in pacifying Yuchi Jiong, he was made Pillar of State and advanced to Duke of Hejian.

literal: In the Kaihuang era of Sui he was made Commander-in-Chief of Yuan Province.
idiomatic: Under Sui Kaihuang he was made Commander-in-Chief of Yuan Province.

literal: A merchant was robbed by bandits; the man suspected a fellow lodger and seized him.
idiomatic: A merchant was robbed by bandits; he suspected a fellow lodger and seized him.

literal: Bao observed that his color showed innocence and his words were upright, and released him.
idiomatic: Bao saw innocence in his face and uprightness in his words, and released him.

literal: The merchant went to the capital to sue Bao for taking gold and releasing the thief.
idiomatic: The merchant went to the capital to accuse Bao of taking gold to let the thief go.

literal: Emperor Wen of Sui sent men to investigate thoroughly; the envoy interrogated Bao on why he took profit in gold and released the robber.
idiomatic: Emperor Wen sent investigators; the envoy pressed Bao on why he had taken gold and freed the robber.

literal: Bao accepted blame without change in his words.
idiomatic: Bao accepted blame without shifting his story.

literal: The envoy and Bao both went to the capital; he was thereupon dismissed from office.
idiomatic: The envoy brought Bao to the capital, and he was dismissed from office.

literal: The thief was soon exposed elsewhere.
idiomatic: The real thief was soon caught elsewhere.

literal: The emperor said: "How could you go so far as to falsely accuse yourself?"
idiomatic: The emperor said, "Why would you go so far as to accuse yourself falsely?"

literal: Bao said: "Your servant received charge of one province and could not quell robbers—my first fault.
idiomatic: Bao said, "I was charged with a whole province and could not suppress robbery—that is my first fault.

literal: The common people were slandered by others, yet I did not hand them to the judicial offices and at once released them—my second fault.
idiomatic: A commoner was slandered, yet I did not hand him to the courts and released him at once—that is my second fault.

literal: Without regard for appearances, I am to this day suspected by others—my third fault.
idiomatic: Without regard for how it looked, I am suspected to this day—that is my third fault.

literal: Your servant has three faults—what escape from punishment is there!
idiomatic: I have three faults—how could I escape blame!

literal: Your servant also did not speak of receiving bribes; the envoy would again have pursued investigation, and then bonds would have spread to touch the innocent—doubling your servant's fault; therefore I falsely accused myself.
idiomatic: Nor did I deny taking a bribe; the envoy would have pressed the inquiry further, and then the innocent would have been dragged into bonds—doubling my fault. That is why I accused myself falsely."

literal: The emperor sighed in wonder and called him an elder of worth.
idiomatic: The emperor marveled and called him a man of true stature.

literal: The Prince of Yueiang, Wanshou, was enfeoffed in the third year of Heping and appointed Grand General Campaigning East, garrisoning Helong.
idiomatic: The Prince of Yueiang, Wanshou, was enfeoffed in the third year of Heping and appointed Grand General Campaigning East, stationed at Helong.

literal: Greedy and violent by nature, on the return from campaign he died of grief on the road; his posthumous title was Prince Li.
idiomatic: Greedy and violent, he died of distress on the road while returning from campaign; his posthumous name was Prince Li.

literal: His son the Prince of Le, Yueping, inherited.
idiomatic: His son the Prince of Le, Yueping, inherited.

literal: He died.
idiomatic: He died.

literal: His son Changming inherited.
idiomatic: His son Changming inherited.

literal: For killing a man he was granted death; the state was abolished.
idiomatic: For murder he was sentenced to death and the fief was abolished.

literal: His son Zhong, in Emperor Ming's time, had the former title restored and held the office of Vice Director of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices.
idiomatic: His son Zhong, in Emperor Ming's time, had the former title restored and served as Vice Director of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices.

literal: Emperor Xiaowu floated on the Tianquan Pool and ordered the princes of the imperial clan to accompany the feast.
idiomatic: Emperor Xiaowu boated on the Tianquan Pool and ordered the imperial princes to join the feast.

literal: Zhong was stupid and without wisdom, and by nature loved clothes; he therefore wore a red silk jacket embroidered at the collar, green silk trousers, and brocade trim.
idiomatic: Zhong was dull and witless and loved fine dress; he wore a red silk jacket with embroidered collar, green silk trousers, and brocade trim.

literal: The emperor said to him: "Court dress and caps ought to have a fixed form—why wear the clothes of street performers?"
idiomatic: The emperor said, "Court dress has its proper form—why are you dressed like a street performer?"

literal: Zhong said: "What your servant has loved since youth remains in brocade and gauze; singing robes and dancing garments are what your servant desires."
idiomatic: Zhong said, "What I have loved since youth lives in silk and gauze—singing robes and dancing dress are what I want."

literal: The emperor said: "That a man can be so without conscience—indeed it reaches this!"
idiomatic: The emperor said, "That a man can be so utterly without shame—it truly comes to this!"

literal: The Prince of Guangping, Luohou, was enfeoffed in the second year of Heping.
idiomatic: The Prince of Guangping, Luohou, was enfeoffed in the second year of Heping.

literal: He died; his posthumous title was Shang.
idiomatic: He died with the posthumous title Shang.

literal: He had no son; later the fifth son of the Prince of Yangping You, Kuang, was made his heir.
idiomatic: He had no son; later the fifth son of the Prince of Yangping You, Kuang, was made his heir.

literal: Kuang, courtesy name Jianfu, was upright and possessed moral fiber.
idiomatic: Kuang, courtesy name Jianfu, was upright and possessed moral fiber.

literal: Emperor Xiaowen valued him.
idiomatic: Emperor Xiaowen valued him.

literal: He said to him: "Uncle, you will surely be able to set the form of the altars of state and support and assist Our person; now you may change your name to Kuang, to fulfill the beauty of bringing the enterprise to completion."
idiomatic: He told him, "Uncle, you will surely uphold the altars and assist my person; you may now change your name to Kuang—to fulfill the beauty of seeing the work through to the end."

literal: When Emperor Xuanwu took the throne he was repeatedly promoted to Attendant of the Yellow Gate in charge of matters.
idiomatic: When Emperor Xuanwu took the throne he rose to Attendant of the Yellow Gate in charge of matters.

literal: Ru Hao first gained favor; the hundred officials slightly feared him.
idiomatic: When Ru Hao first gained favor, the hundred officials feared him somewhat.

literal: The emperor once on returning from the mountain tomb ordered Kuang to accompany the carriage, and also had Hao mount the vehicle.
idiomatic: Once, returning from the imperial tombs, the emperor ordered Kuang to ride beside him and also had Hao mount the carriage.

literal: Hao lifted his robe to ascend; Kuang remonstrated; the emperor pushed him down and made him descend; Hao hated Kuang and turned pale.
idiomatic: Hao lifted his robe to climb in; Kuang remonstrated; the emperor pushed Hao down; Hao hated Kuang and turned pale.

literal: At the time they admired his loyal bluntness.
idiomatic: At the time all admired his blunt loyalty.

literal: When Emperor Xuanwu personally took government he was made Governor of Si Province.
idiomatic: When Emperor Xuanwu took personal rule he was made Governor of Si.

literal: Kuang, having offended Hao, feared being harmed by him and cultivated himself with integrity and caution, gaining a very fine reputation and record.
idiomatic: Having offended Hao, Kuang feared harm and governed with scrupulous integrity, earning a fine reputation.

literal: He was transferred to Governor of Heng Province.
idiomatic: He was transferred to Governor of Heng.

literal: He was summoned as Director of the Imperial Clan and Rectifier of the Right for Henan.
idiomatic: He was summoned as Director of the Imperial Clan and Rectifier of the Right for Henan.

literal: Kuang memorialized that imperial princes and the consorts of the founding princes and second-rank princes all ought to have the title of consort.
idiomatic: Kuang memorialized that imperial princes' wives and those of the founding and second-rank princes should all bear the title consort.

literal: Yet for princes below the third rank they were all called "wife."
idiomatic: Yet for princes below the third rank they were all called simply "wife."

literal: Above they could not share the same title of consort, while below they fell short of the fifth rank and above having the title of ennobled lady—he privately regarded this as doubtful.
idiomatic: They could not share the consort title above, yet fell short of the ennobled ladies granted from fifth rank upward—he found this inconsistent.

literal: An edict said: "When the husband is honored at court, the wife is glorified in the chamber; for women there is no fixed rank—they rise with their husbands.
idiomatic: The edict said, "When the husband is honored at court the wife is glorified at home; women have no fixed rank but rise with their husbands.

literal: The third-rank princes have now opened princely enfeoffment; the title of consort ought likewise to be equal.
idiomatic: Third-rank princes now hold princely fiefs; their consorts' titles should be equal as well.

literal: Wife means equal; in principle she is equal to oneself—she may follow the consort precedent.
idiomatic: Wife means equal—in principle she stands equal to her husband—and may follow the consort precedent.

literal: " From then on the titles of third-rank princes' wives were fixed.
idiomatic: From then on the titles of third-rank princes' wives were fixed.

literal: He was next made Minister of Revenue.
idiomatic: He was next made Minister of Revenue.

literal: Kuang memorialized citing the precedents of Leiling and Zhangwu, requesting to continue Luohou's enfeoffment.
idiomatic: Kuang memorialized citing the precedents of Leiling and Zhangwu, asking to inherit Luohou's fief.

literal: An edict was sent to the Masters of Writing for deliberation.
idiomatic: An edict referred the matter to the Masters of Writing for deliberation.
